nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: Why might cities prefer to use incentives instead of rules for climate action?
nodes.answer: Incentives help guide behavior without overtly controlling it, which can be beneficial when cities lack power over certain emissions sources.
nodes.paragraph: While we are interested in what sectors are covered by CAPs, we also seek to better understand the types of strategies employed. Here, we under - stand climate change as a collective action problem (Ostrom 2010 ; Hormio 2023 ) and thus define a strategy typology under policy mechanisms for solving collective action problems: rules, incentives, and norms (Young 2013 ). Each of these three policy tools present opportunities and challenges for city climate action. For instance, when an emissions source falls under a city S jurisdictional powers, new rules can be an efficient path towards rapid GHG reduction. However, environmental regulations can be controversial and easily politicized in the U.S. (Hanna and McDonald 2021 ; Basseches et al. 2022 ), and the majority of community emissions may originate from sectors that cities lack the power to control. In this case, incentives can become a popular option as they help guide but don t overtly control the behavior of private sector and civil society actors. On the other hand, cities require sufficient resources to offer powerful incen - tives, and high emitters must weigh whether an incentive program can adequately cover their costs to reduce emissions.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What is deemed preferable in scenarios of negative policy cost regarding rebates?
nodes.answer: A negative flat-rate charge (i.e., a lump-sum rebate) is preferable to a negative consumption surcharge in the majority of circumstances.
nodes.paragraph: Some policies stipulatethat the generator return this windfall to the governing body. This can result in a negative policy cost, or a rebate for consumers (e.g. Government of Ireland 2020b ). 3We consider this scenario in our analysis. We nd that, for scenarios of positive cost, ef ciency grows in relative importance as the magnitude of the subsidy burden increases. However, for the scenarios analysed, equity stilloutweighs the ef ciency loss given likely social aversion towards inequality. An energy pricesurcharge is preferable to a at-rate charge, therefore. For scenarios of negative policy cost,the converse is true and a negative at-rate charge (i.e., a lump-sum rebate) is preferable to anegative consumption surcharge (i.e., a reduction in the volumetric price) in the majority ofcircumstances. The welfare maximising cost-recovery option is therefore largely predicatedon whether one expects the long-term cost trajectory to be positive or negative. 1For the 2015/16 Irish scenario, an electricity price surcharge shifts the burden from those with lower incomes towards those with higher incomes 2While energy subsidies are most commonly employed to support renewable energy (for discussion, see Farrell and Lyons 2015 ), energy subsidies and the associated cost-recovery mechanisms can often be used to support household-level energy ef ciency investment (for discussion, see Chawla and Pollitt 2013 ).
